claims.text: The baseline is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with its natural Cu distribution.
A controlled heat treatment or compositional adjustment can increase the volume fraction of Cu-rich precipitates in the coating.
The intervention can make the Cu-rich precipitates more uniformly distributed.
Thermal exposure in the high-temperature sliding regime facilitates oxidation.
Thermal exposure in the high-temperature sliding regime alters deformation mechanisms.
Cu-rich precipitates act as local oxidation-nucleation sites during high-temperature sliding.
Increasing and homogenizing Cu-rich precipitates promotes formation of a protective oxide layer.
Cu-rich precipitates accelerate formation of a stable and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
The oxide layer mechanically reinforces the coating and impedes shear deformation.
Localized hardening and the improved oxide scale reduce microscopic plastic deformation relative to the baseline coating.
Localized hardening and the improved oxide scale reduce overall wear relative to the baseline coating.
The Cu-enhanced coating will have a significantly lower high-temperature sliding wear rate than the baseline coating.
The Cu-enhanced coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation, including reduced grain-boundary sliding or dislocation activity, than the baseline coating.
The predicted benefits are limited to high-temperature sliding conditions and may disappear at lower temperatures because oxidation kinetics and deformation mechanisms differ.

Failure of the precipitate-enhanced coating to produce a statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and microscopic plastic deformation under matched high-temperature sliding conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
